title: San Jose Seventh-Grader Boosts Air-to-Water Output 117%, Reaches National STEM Final
excerpt: Ankith Burki built an atmospheric water generator from scratch, found that low-frequency sound waves dramatically increased its water collection, and earned a finalist spot in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge.
body:
• Ankith Burki, a seventh-grader from San Jose, California, built his own atmospheric water generator and found that low-frequency sine waves increased its water collection by 117%.
  • The prototype uses the Peltier thermoelectric effect to cool surrounding air by 7.5°C below the dew point; he ran four-hour trials — five silent, ten with sound — testing sine and triangle waveforms.
  • The project earned him a place among 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge; finalists travel to Washington, DC, October 23–28 for Finals Week, with $100,000-plus in prizes at stake.
  • Burki, also a Carnatic classical vocalist, says he hopes to become an environmental engineer and sees his science as a way to help people who have fewer resources.

For Ankith Burki, a seventh-grader from San Jose, the global water crisis was never just a classroom topic. He built an atmospheric water generator from scratch, then asked a question few researchers had bothered to test: could sound make it better? The answer, measured across dozens of hours of trials, was striking — low-frequency sine waves increased the device's water collection by 117%. The project has now carried him into the finals of the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge, the premier national STEM competition for middle-school students in the United States, according to the Society for Science.

The experiment

Burki designed and assembled his own prototype using the Peltier effect, a thermoelectric process in which an electric current moves heat from one side of a material to another. After several rounds of trials, he produced a device capable of lowering the temperature around it by 7.5°C — enough to push humid air below its dew point, the threshold at which water vapour condenses into droplets that can be captured and measured.

Then came the real experiment: four-hour tests, five silent for a baseline and ten with low-frequency sound from a speaker, comparing sine and triangle waveforms. The idea was simple — vibrations could help tiny droplets merge into larger ones that fall into the collector. Under low-frequency sine waves, the device collected 117% more water than in the silent tests, suggesting sound could be a low-cost efficiency boost — though more research is needed before the technique leaves the lab.

Why the problem matters

The starting point for Burki's project is a sobering figure: more than 4 billion people do not have sufficient access to fresh water, and climate change is expected to deepen water stress in many regions. Atmospheric water generators — devices that pull drinkable moisture directly from humid air — offer one possible answer, because they reduce dependence on conventional water sources. But many existing generators do not produce enough water to be practical for the communities that need them most. That efficiency gap is exactly what Burki set out to narrow.

The Challenge rewards students who identify meaningful problems, test their ideas carefully, and explain how their work could matter beyond the lab. The Society for Science named the 30 finalists on September 16; they gather in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, where each receives a $500 award and competes for more than $100,000 in prizes.

Young India, global laboratory

For Indian-American families, stories like Burki's carry a particular resonance. Atmospheric water technology is not an abstract concern for the diaspora — India faces some of the world's most severe water stress, and improvements in low-cost water harvesting have direct relevance to the villages and cities many immigrants left behind. The Indian diaspora has a deep bench of young achievers in American science competitions, and Burki's project stands out for taking on a problem whose solution would matter as much in Tamil Nadu or Rajasthan as in California.

There is a quieter thread, too: Burki performs Indian Carnatic classical vocal music, a practice he has described as soothing and rooted in generations of tradition. The link is almost poetic — an experiment about the physics of sound from a boy raised on its music.

What's next

Finals Week in late October will decide whether the project earns a top prize. Longer term, Burki wants to become an environmental engineer, and has said his own comfortable life comes with a responsibility to build solutions for those with fewer resources. The prototype is not a finished answer — energy use, humidity needs and scale remain obstacles — but a 117% jump under test conditions opens a new question about what sound can do for water harvesting.
